subject: SQL
text: Welcome to the SQL Tutorial, presented to you by 1Keydata.com.

subject: SQL
text: In this tutorial, we will go over the basics of SQL, so you'll be able to use SQL to write

subject: SQL
text: simple queries to get data from a relational database.

subject: SQL
text: We will first provide some background information on how data gets stored in a relational database.

subject: SQL
text: Next we will go over the basic SQL commands.

subject: SQL
text: In particular, you will learn about:

subject: SQL
text: SELECT / FROM WHERE

subject: SQL
text: ORDER BY GROUP BY

subject: SQL
text: HAVING

subject: SQL
text: In a relational database, data is stored in tables.

subject: SQL
text: Each table has a table name.

subject: SQL
text: A table consists of columns and rows.

subject: SQL
text: Each column is a field in a record, and there is a column name associated with each column.

subject: SQL
text: Each row represents one record.

subject: SQL
text: Usually when we say how many records we have, we are referring to the number of rows.

subject: SQL
text: With this information, now we are ready to dive into SQL.

subject: SQL
text: SQL is structured very much like the English language.

subject: SQL
text: At the high level, the basic command for retrieving data from a database table is to SELECT data

subject: SQL
text: FROM a table.

subject: SQL
text: Not surprisingly, the keywords "SELECT" and "FROM" make up the core of the SQL statement.

subject: SQL
text: In fact, the syntax for SELECT FROM is pretty straightforward: SELECT COLUMN_NAME FROM TABLE_NAME.

subject: SQL
text: We can select one or more columns.

subject: SQL
text: To select more than one column, we simply list all the column names we want to select

subject: SQL
text: separated by comma.

subject: SQL
text: If we want to select all columns, we say SELECT *.

subject: SQL
text: If we want to select unique values, we add the keyword DISTINCT in front of the column

subject: SQL
text: name.

subject: SQL
text: Next we look at the WHERE keyword.

subject: SQL
text: In the previous example, we are retrieving all records from a table.

subject: SQL
text: While we do want to do this sometimes, more frequently we want to select only a subset

subject: SQL
text: of the data.

subject: SQL
text: When we want to filter our results, we use the WHERE keyword after the FROM keywords.

subject: SQL
text: So the syntax becomes

subject: SQL
text: SELECT COLUMN_NAME FROM TABLE_NAME WHERE [Condition]

subject: SQL
text: Condition is where we specify how we want the data to be filtered.

subject: SQL
text: For example, we may specify that only people whose first name starts with "A" is selected.

subject: SQL
text: Now we turn our attention to the ORDER BY keyword.

subject: SQL
text: Sometimes we want the output to be listed in a particular order, such as in ascending

subject: SQL
text: order or in descending order.

subject: SQL
text: To achieve this, we use the OREDER BY keyword.

subject: SQL
text: The syntax for this will be something similar to the following:

subject: SQL
text: SELECT COLUMN_NAME FROM TABLE_NAME WHERE [Condition] ORDER BY COLUMN_NAME either ASC or DESC

subject: SQL
text: Notice that ORDER BY is at the end of the statement, because we want to specify the

subject: SQL
text: ordering after we have specified what data we want to get.

subject: SQL
text: To show results in ascending order, i.e., from A to Z or from smaller values to larger

subject: SQL
text: values, we can add ASC at the end.

subject: SQL
text: To show results in descending order, i.e., from Z to A or from larger values to smaller

subject: SQL
text: values, we can add DESC at the end.

subject: SQL
text: Usually if you do not specify this, the default is ascending.

subject: SQL
text: Next we discuss the GROUP BY keyword.

subject: SQL
text: Before we go into details about GROUP BY, I'd like to talk first about functions.

subject: SQL
text: The typical mathematical functions you see in SQL are SUM, AVG, COUNT, MAX, and MIN.

subject: SQL
text: Functions allow us to operate on the values of specific columns.

subject: SQL
text: For example, the MAX function allows us to retrieve the largest value in a column.

subject: SQL
text: Let's say we have a table that has three columns: Date, Store, and Sales Amount.

subject: SQL
text: To find out what was the highest sales amount across all dates and all stores, we can simply

subject: SQL
text: use SELECT MAX(Sales Amount).

subject: SQL
text: On the other hand, if we want to find out the highest sales amount for each store, then

subject: SQL
text: we'll need to retrieve both the Store column and the sales amount column, and our SELECT

subject: SQL
text: statement becomes

subject: SQL
text: SELECT Store, MAX(Sales Amount)

subject: SQL
text: However, this SELECT statement by itself is not enough.

subject: SQL
text: To allow SQL to correctly calculate what we want, we need to use the GROUP BY keyword.

subject: SQL
text: Here, we will add

subject: SQL
text: GROUP BY Store

subject: SQL
text: to let SQL know that we want to calculate the maximum sales amount for each store.

subject: SQL
text: So how the function is calculated is dependent on the column or columns specified in the

subject: SQL
text: GROUP BY, not the column or columns specified in the SELECT.

subject: SQL
text: Often the columns in the GROUP BY phrase are same as the columns in the SELECT statement,

subject: SQL
text: but this is not always the case.

subject: SQL
text: To recap, the general syntax for GROUP BY is

subject: SQL
text: SELECT ¡§COLUMN_NAME1¡¨, FUNCTION(¡§COLUMN_NAME2¡¨) FROM ¡§TABLE_NAME¡¨

subject: SQL
text: GROUP BY ¡§COLUMN_NAME1¡¨

subject: SQL
text: Previously we had talked about using the WHERE keyword to filter results.

subject: SQL
text: What if we want to filter based on the result of a function?

subject: SQL
text: Can we also use WHERE for this?

subject: SQL
text: The answer is no, and the reason is that we will need to specify the filtering condition

subject: SQL
text: after SQL has calculated the function, and as a result any filtering condition based

subject: SQL
text: on the function needs to be specified after the GROUP BY phrase.

subject: SQL
text: So we cannot use the WHERE keyword because it is always used before GROUP BY.

subject: SQL
text: This is where the HAVING keyword comes in.

subject: SQL
text: The syntax for HAVING is

subject: SQL
text: SELECT ¡§COLUMN NAME 1¡¨, FUNCTION(¡§COLUMN NAME 2¡¨)

subject: SQL
text: FROM ¡§TABLE_NAME¡¨ GROUP BY ¡§COLUMN NAME 1¡¨

subject: SQL
text: HAVING (Condition based on Function)

subject: SQL
text: In the example we had previously mentioned, if we only want to show results where the

subject: SQL
text: maximum sales amount is over 100, we will add

subject: SQL
text: HAVING (sales Amount > 100) at the end of the SQL query.

subject: SQL
text: In this tutorial we have introduced the SELECT FROM, WHERE, ORDER BY, GROUP BY, and HAVING

subject: SQL
text: keywords.

subject: SQL
text: In a SQL statement, what order do we put them?

subject: SQL
text: The correct order is SELECT FROM, then WHERE, then GROUP BY, then HAVING, and finally ORDER

subject: SQL
text: BY.

subject: SQL
text: That concludes this SQL tutorial.

subject: SQL
text: Thank you for viewing.

subject: SQL
text: Now you have the knowledge to write basic SQL statements to get data out of a relational

subject: SQL
text: database.

subject: SQL
